opus-5.5.text:
I think the main worry for me is about what happens to the usual checks on state power once the state no longer really needs its citizens.

Historically, governments have had to keep their populations at least somewhat on side, because they depend on people to staff the bureaucracy, the army, and the police, and to generate the tax base. Even fairly authoritarian regimes have to worry about the generals, the civil servants, and whether people will show up to work. That dependence is a big part of why states end up being somewhat responsive to human interests, even when nobody planned it that way.

If you have a government-run AGI programme that succeeds, a lot of that dependence goes away. The state can increasingly substitute AI for the people it used to rely on. And a government project means the most powerful systems are developed inside an institution that already holds a monopoly on legitimate force, often with secrecy justified by national security. So you lose some of the friction you'd get from having multiple competing labs, journalists poking around, employees who might blow the whistle, and so on.

People sometimes say a government programme would at least be more accountable than a private company. I understand the appeal, but accountability mechanisms like elections, courts, and a free press work partly because the people in those institutions have independent bargaining power. Once the AI systems are doing most of the work, those mechanisms can stay in place on paper while becoming hollow in practice.

To be clear, I don't think the private-lab path is safe either. This is part of what I've been calling gradual disempowerment: even without any dramatic coup or misaligned AI takeover, the structural incentives keeping our institutions aligned with human interests could quietly erode. A centralised government programme concentrates that risk and potentially speeds it up. And it's very hard to undo, because whoever holds that capability would have both the means and the motive to keep holding it.

r001.rationale: The response says a government AGI capability would be hard to undo because its holder would have the means and motive to retain it. It does not identify capture by someone indifferent to safety or the public good, or compare how difficult recovery would be.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that worries me most is that it doesn't actually solve the problem people think it solves. The usual pitch is: right now we've got a handful of companies racing each other, cutting corners on safety, and the fix is to nationalise it, put it under democratic control, and let the adults run it. And I'm sympathetic to the diagnosis. But I think the cure imports most of the same dynamics and adds a few new ones.

The first issue is that a government programme is still in a race. It's just racing against other governments instead of other companies, and that race is, if anything, more intense, because now it's framed as a national security question. And once something is a national security question, a lot of the mechanisms we'd normally rely on to keep it honest start to get switched off. You get classification, you get reduced external scrutiny, you get a culture where raising concerns is seen as disloyalty rather than diligence. The Manhattan Project analogy that people reach for is actually a decent illustration of this. That was a programme that was very good at building the thing and not very good at deliberating about whether or how to use it.

The second thing, and this is the one I spend more time thinking about, is what happens after it works. Suppose a government succeeds in building systems that can do most cognitively demanding work. The thing that has historically kept governments responsive to their citizens is that governments need people. They need workers to run the economy, they need soldiers, they need taxpayers, they need the cooperation of a lot of humans to get anything done. That dependence is the real mechanism behind a lot of what we call accountability. If you remove it, if the state can run its economy and its military with systems it controls directly, then the incentives that push towards treating people well get a lot weaker. Not because anyone's evil, but because the structural reason to care is gone.

And a government AGI programme is kind of the maximally concentrated version of that. You've taken the most powerful capability in history and put it under the control of a single institution that also has a monopoly on force. With companies you at least have the possibility of multiple actors, some competition, some ability to exit. A single state programme, if it actually achieves what it sets out to achieve, is close to the end state I'm most nervous about, which is one entity that no longer needs anyone's consent to do what it wants.

So I'm not saying leave it all to the labs. I think there's a real role for government in things like verification, in setting the rules of the game, in international coordination that stops the race in the first place. What I'm sceptical of is the idea that just moving the project into a government building fixes the underlying problem. The underlying problem is concentration of power combined with the removal of the reasons that power has historically had to answer to anyone. A government programme doesn't address that. In a lot of ways, it's the clearest route to it.

r001.rationale: The response warns that a state AGI programme could concentrate power in one institution and weaken accountability, but it does not identify capture by someone indifferent to safety or the public good, or the comparative difficulty of recovering from such capture.

astra-6.text:
What worries me is that putting AGI development inside a government doesn’t automatically solve the alignment problem. You still have to figure out how to keep these systems under control. But now you may also have secrecy, national-security pressure, and a sense that you absolutely cannot let the other side get there first. That seems like a difficult environment in which to say, “We don’t understand what’s happening, and we need to stop.”

There’s also the question of who gets control if the programme succeeds. A system could be doing exactly what its operators want and still be disastrous for everyone else. So I’d want to distinguish keeping an AGI under human control from making sure that the humans controlling it are accountable. A government programme needs credible answers to both.

r001.rationale: The response discusses government secrecy, national-security pressure, and accountability, but does not identify capture by someone indifferent to safety or the public good, or the comparative difficulty of recovering from that capture.

sol-6.1.text:
What worries me is that putting an AGI programme under government control doesn’t by itself solve the problem of control. You still have to ask: who within the government actually understands what the system is doing? Who can challenge the claims being made about it? And can anyone stop the programme once it becomes a matter of national security?

I can imagine a dynamic where everyone involved thinks, “This is dangerous, but the other side is going to do it, so we have to get there first.” Then secrecy makes it harder to scrutinise the technical work, and competition makes it harder to slow down. You could have very conscientious people participating in a process that none of them individually thinks is sensible.

There’s also the concentration of power. Even if you solved the technical problem of making an AGI follow instructions, it matters enormously whose instructions it follows. A system that faithfully serves a small group of people could still be a terrible outcome for everyone else. So I’d want to distinguish making these systems controllable from making the institutions controlling them accountable.

r001.rationale: The response raises concentration of power and accountability, but does not identify the comparative difficulty of recovering from capture by someone indifferent to safety or the public good.
